title: Nanakuli Paving & Rock Co. v. Shell Oil Co.
summary: The jury could find that established price protection qualified Shell’s posted-price term and that imposing a sudden increase violated commercial standards of good faith.
notes:
The editors compare Naval Institute: industry practice cannot simply erase an agreed restriction on early paperback sales. They also ask whether a comparable usage could explain irrevocability of a subcontractor’s bid in Drennan. That latter question is an editorial comparison, not a Nanakuli holding.

The dispute arose from Shell's 1974 price increase, which it announced by letter giving Nanakuli one day's notice; the Ninth Circuit (664 F.2d 772 (9th Cir. 1981)) held that price protection was a universal practice in the Hawaiian asphaltic paving trade because government paving contracts lacked escalation clauses.

sections.Parties: Nanakuli, a Hawaiian paving contractor, bought its asphalt from Shell. Nanakuli sued after Shell imposed a price increase on asphalt required for paving work already committed at earlier prices.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties had dealt under asphalt-supply agreements since 1963. Their 1969 agreement specified Shell’s posted price at the time of delivery. Nanakuli bid for public and private paving work at fixed prices; the relevant public contracts did not allow an increase simply because asphalt became more expensive. Evidence showed that suppliers to the local paving trade commonly protected customers against increases on work already committed. Protection could take the form of advance notice or continued sales at the old price for a specified quantity or period.

Shell had protected Nanakuli on the two earlier price increases under the agreement, in 1970 and 1971. Its records discussed the extent of protection to be given. In the disputed increase, Shell raised the price from $44 to $76 per ton effective January 1, 1974, in a letter dated December 31 that arrived January 4. Nanakuli needed 7,200 tons for work committed on the old basis. Another asphalt supplier, Chevron, had given substantial advance notice of its increase.
sections.Procedural History: A jury awarded Nanakuli $220,800. The district court entered judgment for Shell notwithstanding the verdict. The Ninth Circuit reversed and reinstated the jury’s award, with interest. Judge Kennedy concurred separately, emphasizing the need for established objective standards and notice.
sections.Issue: Could trade usage and the parties’ performance qualify the written posted-price term, and could the manner of imposing the increase independently violate the duty of good faith?
sections.Holding: Yes. The evidence permitted the jury to find for Nanakuli on either theory. Price protection could be reasonably consistent with the express price term, and Shell’s method of implementing the increase could fall below reasonable commercial standards.
sections.Reasoning:
The UCC treats the agreement as broader than the writing alone. Regular commercial practices and the parties’ own performance can explain, supplement, or qualify express terms. The relevant trade could include suppliers to the Hawaiian paving industry, rather than only sellers of asphalt. Evidence from that local market supported a sufficiently established expectation of protection.

The posted price remained the ordinary price. An exception protecting previously committed work during an increase did not wholly displace it. The jury also could treat Shell’s earlier protection as evidence of the agreement’s meaning, rather than merely as voluntary waivers. A preference for construing ambiguous acts as waivers did not require that characterization when the evidence supported a course of performance.

The alternative good-faith theory focused on timing and implementation, not simply the size of the price. A posted price ordinarily can satisfy the Code, but Shell’s sudden effective date, delayed notice, and refusal to protect existing bids could violate the commercial standards proved in this record. The appellate court upheld a permissible jury finding; it did not announce that every supplier must provide price protection.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Nanakuli connects interpretation, evidence of prior performance, and good-faith limits on contractual discretion. It shows why the written price clause is the beginning of an inquiry into the agreement rather than the entire inquiry.

topics.assent: The agreement includes sufficiently established commercial understandings as well as the written words.
topics.interpretation: Price protection qualifies the ordinary posted-price term without entirely replacing it.
topics.trade-usage: The court permits proof of a local paving-industry practice and the parties’ own course of performance.
topics.good-faith: The manner and timing of a price increase can violate the standards applicable to a merchant.
topics.discretion: Shell’s ability to set a posted price did not settle whether it could implement that price without the protection expected in this trade.
topics.course-dealing: Shell's price protection on the 1970 and 1971 increases was treated as course of performance/course of dealing reinforcing the trade usage.

learning.separateOpinions: Judge Kennedy stressed that neither interpretation nor good faith should allow a jury to invent a specific protection from general fairness alone. Well-established custom or another objective standard, of which the parties had clear notice, supplied the necessary foundation here.
